newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Ericsson seen on course for growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ericsson seen on course for growth.

text.p: LM Ericsson AB on Tuesday met market expectations with a 30 percent jump in nine month profits which boosted hopes that the Swedish telecoms giant would ring up further growth, led by its mobile phone unit.

Ericsson reported a nine month pre-tax profit of 6.26 billion crowns ($954 million) against 4.81 billion a year ago but rang a warning note that increasing competition in the global telecoms sector could impact profit margins.
The company said order bookings had risen 22 percent in the nine months to 95.63 billion crowns and net sales by 17 percent to 78.20 billion crowns - largely due to its mobile phone unit.
"This was a good, solid set of numbers," analyst Peter Knox from UBS told Reuters.
"There is clear evidence of continuing strong order intake ...with the trend looking increasingly positive."

Analysts were expecting the strong trend in order bookings to continue in the fourth quarter. Chief executive Lars Ramqvist told a news conference order bookings could reach 130 billion crowns for the full year.
The highlight of the report was the radio communications division that includes the company's mobile telephone business and accounted for over 63 percent of sales.
Ericsson's chief executive Lars Ramqvist said sales of mobile phones and systems jumped 38 percent in the nine months to September 30 and order bookings rose 34 percent.
"This means that Ericsson is strengthening its market position," Ramqvist said in a statement.
However he sounded a warning that competition at the cutting edge of mobile telephones could hit profit margins.
U.S. rival Motorala posted weaker third quarter results earlier this month, partly blaming competitive pressures and continuing price declines in cellular telephones.

"Ericsson's gross margin weakened slightly (in the nine months) due to increased competition and continuous consideration has been given in the accounts for increased risks related to changes in technology and markets and greater financial exposure," the company said in the report.
But Knox said Ericsson had a clear advantage over Motorola.
"This is due to the increased exposure in the European market in GSM and digital as a whole," Knox said.
"It is evident that the drive is the radio business."
Analyst Susan Anthony from Schroeders, which has Ericsson on an outperform and buy trading recommendation, said the market was well informed about the sector's rising competition.
"All along they have been warning us to expect tougher competition," Anthony told Reuters. "But if anything it has been less tough than expected."

Analysts said Ericssons' public telecommunications division, which is the company's second largest unit accounting for about 20 percent of sales, saw sales decline to 15.47 billion crowns from 16.35 billion and profitability weak.
Ericsson said this slide was due to strong pressure on prices and delays in China but added a process of change, designed to shorten lead times and cut costs, was continuing.
"We know this is a difficult area and that it is the biggest danger for them," Anthony said.
"But 1996 was always going to be a year of restructuring, of getting things better adjusting for market needs."
Ericsson's share price slipped a touch on the result, trading 4.5 crowns lower ahead of the announcement but was 4.0 crowns lower at 185 crowns at 1440 GMT.
